newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia, Yugoslavia close to restoring traffic.
newsitem.headline: Croatia, Yugoslavia close to restoring traffic.

text.p: Croatia and Yugoslavia agreed on Tuesday to speed up the normalisation of relations following the 1991-95 war and set a mid-June target for agreement on restoring full road and rail traffic.

Foreign Ministers Mate Granic of Croatia and Milan Milutinovic of Yugoslavia met for the third time since the former Balkan foes signed a normalisation agreement in August 1996 after the war that followed the secession of Croatia.

"The essence of my coming to Zagreb today is to help our talks as we realised that in some segments they got a bit 'stuck', so to speak, and that they need certain impetus," Milutinovic told reporters after the talks.
Granic said all the political obstacles were removed for finalising agreements that would allow the full liberalisation of border crossing and rail and road traffic between the two countries.
"We believe that this group of agreements will be finalised in June," Granic said, adding that he would come to Belgrade to sign the accords as soon as the expert groups prepare them.
A Croatian Foreign Ministry official said the two sides agreed to set a mid-June target for finishing the talks.
Granic said some 20 bilateral agreements were briefly discussed at the meeting, saying one on economic cooperation was also close to signing.
Other unresolved issues on which some progress was made at the talks include claims on property on the territory of the other state and the problem of pensioners.
Granic blamed the slow pace of solving outstanding issues on differences in priorities of the two sides, saying: "The problem is in the balance of interest."
Milutinovic said the top Yugoslav priority is the return of Serb refugees now sheltering in Yugoslavia who fled from central Croatia after Zagreb crushed their rebellion in 1995.

Granic said Zagreb does not question the right of all refugees to return to their homes, but that the process has to be an agreed and organised one: "The return of refugees is a legal but also political, economic and security question."
He said the two sides expressed satisfaction with the process of the peaceful reintegration of Eastern Slavonia, the last Serb-held enclave in Croatia due to return to Zagreb rule in July.
